claims.text: A StatefulSet gives each Pod a stable name (db-0) and, through volumeClaimTemplates, its own claim (data-db-0) that a replacement Pod mounts; it does not replicate data between Pods, archive WAL, promote a standby or upgrade PostgreSQL.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Workloads > StatefulSets (Stable network ID, Stable storage); k8s.l2.statefulsets claims

claims.text: With replicas: 2, db-1 would be a second, empty PostgreSQL server with its own claim that receives nothing from db-0; replicas: 1 means one server and no standby.
claims.source_hint: k8s.l2.statefulsets outline item 6 and claims; kubernetes.io StatefulSets (volumeClaimTemplates per Pod)

claims.text: A PostgreSQL standby applies the primary's changes (streaming replication) and can be promoted to accept writes when the primary fails.
claims.source_hint: postgresql.org docs 17: High Availability, Load Balancing, and Replication > Log-Shipping Standby Servers; Failover (pg_promote)

claims.text: A new major version of PostgreSQL cannot start on the data directory of an older major version; the data must be upgraded with pg_upgrade or dumped and restored (or moved by logical replication).
claims.source_hint: postgresql.org docs 17: Server Setup and Operation > Upgrading a PostgreSQL Cluster

claims.text: A managed database runs outside the cluster; apps in the cluster reach it by host name and port like any outside server, so for the api only the database address in its config (ConnectionStrings__Default) changes.
claims.source_hint: glossary managed-database; general description, no provider named (depth_notes)

claims.text: Managed database services usually offer backups and a standby as settings (hedged: no doc in versions.yaml covers providers), and the provider decides some server settings and when maintenance happens; the data lives on the provider's machines.
claims.source_hint: general description of managed database services; no provider named (depth_notes); glossary managed-database

claims.text: Opinion: a managed database usually fits a team that rents its machines from a provider with nobody whose job is running databases; running one in the cluster fits when no such service exists (e.g. a bank's own machines) or the data must stay on them.
claims.source_hint: outline item 4; contested view given in section 6 (databases must never run inside Kubernetes)

claims.text: Opinion: whoever took a backup, provider included, only a restore of it shows that it gives the data back and how long that takes against the RTO.

claims.text: kind runs each cluster's nodes as containers. On kind, the default StorageClass standard keeps each volume in a folder on one node, and a Pod using the claim must run on that node; with the node unschedulable the next Pod stays Pending (storage-class.sh).
At stage-3 every cluster, staging included, is a kind cluster on Docker Desktop on the learner's machine; there is no cloud account in the lab.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang STAGE.md stage-3, Clusters and their resources

claims.text: Staging's only scheduled operation on PostgreSQL is the CronJob db-backup (db-backup.yaml), whose dumps go to the claim db-backups on the same node as data-db-0; it dumps PostgreSQL databases only, not RabbitMQ.
RabbitMQ on staging keeps messages waiting in queues on its claim data-rabbitmq-0; stateful-staging.sh places an order and finds it and its waiting message after deleting db-0 and rabbitmq-0.
claims.source_hint: k8s.l2.staging-keeps-its-data lesson and claims; scripts/k8s/stateful-staging.sh at stage-3

claims.text: redis.yaml at stage-3: L1-4 comment (no claim, everything in it is a copy of PostgreSQL), L6 kind Deployment, L20-24 one container redis:8.10.2-alpine on port 6379, no volumes.
The api uses Redis by cache-aside; a replaced Redis Pod without a volume starts empty, so the next reads are cache misses served from PostgreSQL.
claims.source_hint: STAGE.md stage-3 data flow (API -> cache-aside -> Redis); redis.io docs: persistence (no persistence without a data volume)
